title: CFA Ethics 40: Standard VI(C) - a referral fee must be disclosed whichever way it flows
subtitle: Receiving fees, paying fees, and the arrangements that are not money at all
whyItMatters: This standard is short and often dismissed as paperwork, but it handles a very real conflict: a referral with a financial motive behind it sounds exactly like disinterested advice.
openingQuestion: You refer a client to another wealth management firm and receive a referral fee. What is your duty?
openingOptions: No duty at all, since you no longer serve that client
Disclose the existence and nature of that fee to the client
Telling your own employer about it is quite enough
Disclose it only if the client asks you about it
explanation: Standard VI(C) does not prohibit referral fees - the model is lawful and common. It requires disclosure, because without that information a client cannot tell a referral based on service quality from one based on the size of the commission. The duty runs both ways: receiving a fee must be disclosed, and so must paying a fee to whoever referred a client to you. And the scope goes beyond money - a reciprocal referral arrangement, or receiving some service in return, falls within what must be disclosed.

summary.keyIdea: Referral fees are not prohibited - they are required to be disclosed, in both directions, because money flowing either way distorts the motive behind a referral.
summary.commonMistake: Disclosing only when you are the one receiving. Paying a fee to whoever brought the client in has to be told to that same client.

application.title: The moment of disclosure
application.message: Before the client decides, not inside a contract already signed. Disclosure after the decision has no effect at all.

sections.text: Standard VI(C) requires referral fees to be disclosed. The model is lawful and common - the problem is that a client who does not know cannot evaluate the advice they have just received.
Why it has to be said
Without knowing about the fee, a client cannot tell a referral based on service quality from one based on the size of the commission. Both sound identical when spoken.

sections.label: The duty runs both ways
sections.text: Receiving a fee for referring a client elsewhere must be disclosed. Paying a fee to whoever referred the client to you must be disclosed too - the second direction is often forgotten because it feels like it does not affect your own advice.

items: Not only money: reciprocal referral arrangements, services received in return, or any benefit of value all fall within scope.
It must be disclosed BEFORE the client decides, not after they have signed.
It applies to prospective clients as well as current ones - because that is when they are weighing it up.

sections.text: Three forms of referral fee, one duty

sections.title: Cash is not the only thing requiring disclosure
sections.subtitle: The question is whether any benefit flows with the referral, not what form it takes

concepts.def: The form everyone remembers. It must be told before the client decides, including the structure - a one-off payment or a share of assets, because the two create different incentives.
Often forgotten, because money leaving your own pocket feels like it cannot affect the client. But the client needs to know the referral they trusted was paid for.
You send clients to them, they send clients to you. Not a dong changes hands, but there is a benefit and the incentive is identical - so it must still be disclosed.

sections.label: Timing matters as much as content
sections.text: Disclosure has to happen BEFORE the client makes their decision, not in the quarterly report sent afterwards, and not when the client asks. The reason lies in the standard's purpose: this information exists so the client can weigh the advice at its proper weight. Saying it after they have signed leaves the information complete but useless - and that is the violation.

lines: A client may well accept that you are paid a commission.
What they do not accept is discovering it afterwards.

diagram.label: Receiving or paying referral fees is not prohibited
Both directions must be disclosed: received and paid
Disclose before the client decides, not afterwards

realWorldExample.company: The timing of disclosure decides whether disclosure is worth anything
realWorldExample.description: Disclosure has to happen before the client decides to use the service being referred, not in the year-end summary report. A referral fee revealed after the client has already moved their assets across has lost all its effect - what the client needs is information to weigh, and weighing only means something before a decision. This is why the standard names prospective clients explicitly rather than only current ones.

quiz.question: What does Standard VI(C) require for referral fees?
options: Disclosing the existence and nature of the fee to the client
A complete ban on ever receiving referral fees from third parties
Handing the fee over to your employer to administer for you
Disclosure only where the fee exceeds a certain percentage
quiz.explanation: The referral model is lawful and common; what the standard handles is the client's inability to tell disinterested advice from motivated advice. Banning the arrangement outright would remove a legitimate business model rather than fix that problem. Surrendering the fee to your employer is a separate question governed by Standard IV(B), and a percentage threshold would let the person with the conflict decide when the client gets to hear about it.

quiz.question: In which direction does the disclosure duty run?
options: Both: receiving a fee must be told, and so must paying one
Only on receiving, since that is where the conflict lies
Only on paying, since that is a cost the client indirectly bears
Only whichever of the two carries the larger value
quiz.explanation: Paying a referrer also creates a conflict: the client was brought to you because someone was paid, not necessarily because you were the best fit for them. That is why limiting the duty to money coming in misses half the problem, and why the size of the payment cannot be the trigger - a small fee still explains why a particular name was mentioned to a particular client.

quiz.question: What about a reciprocal referral arrangement with no money in it?
options: Only the employer needs telling about it, not the client
No disclosure is needed, since no money changes hands
It must still be disclosed, because it creates a financial incentive
Disclosure only if the two sides signed a formal document first
quiz.explanation: Economic value does not have to arrive as cash - a steady flow of clients coming the other way is a substantial benefit in itself, and it bends the referral in exactly the same direction a commission would. Nor does the duty depend on paperwork: an informal understanding between two firms produces the same incentive as a signed contract, and the client is the person who needs to know about it.

quiz.question: When must a referral fee be disclosed?
options: At any point in the financial year in which the fee arises
In the periodic summary report sent to clients each year end
Immediately after the fee has actually been paid to you
Before the client decides to use the service being referred
quiz.explanation: Information for weighing something is only worth anything before the weighing, so disclosure after the decision is paperwork rather than disclosure. Each of the other three timings shares the same defect: they all place the disclosure after the client has already acted. Tying it to when the money actually arrives is the most tempting of them, and it can be months after the client committed.

quiz.question: Why does the standard explicitly name "prospective clients"?
options: Because someone not yet a client is still deciding on what you say
Because prospective clients usually have no binding contract
Because the rules require records of everyone you have contacted
Because prospective clients are not protected by any other standard
quiz.explanation: The moment a referral has the most influence is precisely before someone has decided, so that is when the duty to disclose matters most. Prospective clients are of course covered by other standards too - suitability and fair dealing among them - and the point has nothing to do with contracts or record-keeping. It is about catching the decision while it is still open.

keyTakeaways: Referral fees are not prohibited - they are required to be disclosed
The duty runs both ways: receiving and paying
The scope includes non-cash benefits and reciprocal arrangements
Disclosure must come before the client decides, not afterwards
It applies to prospective clients as well as current ones

practicePrompt.question: An insurance company offers to pay you a commission for every client you refer who buys their product. What must you do before accepting?
options: Simply make sure that the product genuinely suits the client's needs and objectives
Disclose the arrangement to the client before referring, and tell your employer
Accept it and record it internally so it can be reconciled at a later date
Refuse it outright, since every commission paid by a product provider is prohibited
practicePrompt.explanation: The first option is half right, and that is where it is easy to stop: suitability is Standard III(C)'s requirement, but it does not replace VI(C)'s duty to disclose. Two standards fire here, plus IV(B) because this is compensation beyond salary - and all three have to be done, not one of them chosen.
